title: Retaining walls and structural boundaries (refer to engineer)
audience: Landscape designers, quoters and crew leaders who decide whether a wall, slope change or structural garden element is in scope or must be referred to an engineer, a building surveyor or a licence holder.
learningOutcomes: Identify the features of a site that signal a retaining wall or structural element, such as a level change, a load from a neighbour's ground or a surcharge from a driveway.
Explain why a wall that holds back soil can become a structural matter that needs an engineer, and why height alone is not the only test.
Apply the boundary between landscape work the business may carry out and structural work that must be referred.
Write a referral that describes the site, the drawing needs and the client's decision points without designing the structure.

instruction.heading: Why retaining walls are a structural matter
instruction.body: A retaining wall holds back soil that would otherwise move. It has to resist the pressure of the soil behind it, any water that builds up behind it, and any load placed on the ground above it, such as a driveway, a car, a fence or a neighbour's building. A wall can look modest and still fail. A poorly drained wall can fill with water and push over. A wall that is built on soft ground can settle and tilt. A wall that holds up a neighbour's ground can collapse onto their property. For these reasons, retaining walls are one of the clearest examples of a boundary between landscape design and structural work. The business may plan the planting and finishes, but the structural design and the decision about whether the wall is safe belong to a qualified engineer or other authorised person.

instruction.heading: Recognising a structural element on site
instruction.body: Look at the site before quoting anything. A level change of any size, a slope that the client wants to flatten, a new terrace, a raised bed with a heavy retaining edge, a wall that supports a path or a driveway, and a wall that is close to a building or a boundary all need a closer look. Check whether the ground behind a wall belongs to the client or a neighbour. Check for surcharge, which is any load placed near the top of the wall, such as a car, a shed, a fence or a stockpile of soil. Look for water: downpipes, paths, overland flow and the drainage behind any wall. Note any existing wall, its condition, its materials and any cracking, leaning or bulging. Record these facts on the site plan. Do not assume a wall is safe because it has stood for a long time.

instruction.heading: Where the boundary sits
instruction.body: The boundary depends on the jurisdiction and on the wall's height, location, load and purpose. In Victoria, the Victorian Building Authority practice note dated April 2022 says a retaining wall under 1 metre needs no building permit, unless it forms part of other building work or protects neighbouring land. In New South Wales, a retaining wall built from any material, sitting outside a habitable building, needs a contractor licence when the residential structural landscaping is valued over $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST (page updated 23 June 2026). In Brisbane, building approval is needed for a fence more than 2 metres above natural ground, and the council counts retaining walls within fence height (page undated). Even where no permit or licence is needed, a wall that holds a neighbour's ground, carries a surcharge, sits near a footing or changes drainage may need an engineer's design. Treat the boundary as a referral point, not a number to remember. This lesson does not grant a building, engineering or structural licence or approval.

instruction.heading: Writing the referral and communicating with the client
instruction.body: A referral should give the engineer or building surveyor what they need without designing the structure yourself. Describe the site location, the level change, the height as measured on site, the ground behind and below the wall, any surcharge, the drainage observations, the neighbour's position, the existing wall condition and the client's purpose for the wall. Attach the photographs taken with consent and the site plan. State clearly what the business proposes to do outside the structural element, such as planting or paving, and what it will not do. Tell the client in writing that the wall requires a referral, that the referral may cost money and take time, and that the business will not start the wall until the structural advice and any approval are in place. Record the referral, the date and the client's decision.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the referral and the scope. A competent designer can show where the structural boundary sits on the site plan, explain the features that triggered the referral, and describe what the business will and will not do. Escalate any wall that is cracked, leaning or bulging, any wall that holds a neighbour's ground, any wall near a building or a footing, and any client request to start construction before the referral is complete.

procedure: Record the level changes, slopes, existing walls, surcharge loads and drainage features on the site plan.
Check whether the ground behind or below the proposed wall belongs to the client or a neighbour.
Identify the features that trigger a referral, including height, surcharge, neighbour ground, proximity to buildings and drainage changes.
Check the approval and exemption rules for the jurisdiction and the council, and record the source and date checked (see the references at the start of this lesson).
Mark the wall as referred on the scope, and state the business's in-scope work around it.
Prepare the referral with the site description, measurements, photographs taken with consent and the client's purpose.
Tell the client in writing about the referral, its likely time and cost, and that the wall will not be started until advice and approvals are in place.
Record the referral, the date sent, the response and the client's decision in the project file.

workedExamples.situation: A client wants a raised garden bed 0.8 metres high along the side fence. The soil behind the bed is the client's, but the fence is shared with a neighbour whose ground is lower.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the raised bed in scope, and what needs a referral?
workedExamples.reasoning: A raised bed with a wall under about one metre may still need a check, because it holds soil next to a shared fence and a neighbour's ground. In Victoria, a wall under one metre is generally exempt from a permit unless it protects adjoining property, which this may do. Refer the question to a building surveyor or engineer, record the site facts, and tell the client the bed will not be built until the advice is in. The business may plan the planting in the bed once the structure is cleared.

workedExamples.situation: A crew is asked to build a two-metre retaining wall to level a sloping lawn so that a shed can be placed at the top, close to the boundary.
workedExamples.reasoning: The height, the surcharge from the shed and the proximity to the boundary all point to a structural matter. Do not quote the wall as a landscape item. Refer it to an engineer, explain the referral to the client in writing, and set out what the business can do outside the wall, such as the shed base only if it is cleared by the engineer. Record the referral and wait for the design before any quote for construction.

equipmentAndPpe: Measuring tape, level and survey stakes for measuring the wall line and heights
Camera or phone for photographs taken with consent
Site plan template with level, drainage and surcharge fields
High-visibility clothing and footwear for site visits
Referral template for engineers and building surveyors

commonErrors.error: Quoting a retaining wall as a landscape item without checking its height, surcharge or neighbour impact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the trigger list on the site plan and refer any wall with a trigger before quoting.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a wall under a certain height never needs advice.
commonErrors.prevention: Height is one test. Check surcharge, neighbour ground, drainage, footings and the local rules.

commonErrors.error: Starting to build a wall while the referral is still open.
commonErrors.prevention: Hold all wall work until the engineer's advice and any approvals are in writing.

commonErrors.error: Designing the structure in the referral.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the site and the purpose. Leave the structural design to the qualified person.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Victoria: retaining walls under 1 metre need no building permit unless they form part of other building works or protect neighbouring land (practice note dated April 2022). This is a Victorian position only.

New South Wales: a licence is needed for residential structural landscaping valued over $5,000 including GST, which covers retaining walls outside habitable buildings (page updated 23 June 2026). The page gives no height figure.
Queensland (Brisbane City Council): building approval is needed for fences more than 2 metres above natural ground, with retaining walls counted in fence height (page undated).
Check the wall height rules for the state, territory and council where the wall is built before you build it.
This lesson does not grant any building, engineering, structural or building-surveyor licence or approval, and it does not authorise the business to design a retaining wall.
Collapse of a retaining wall can injure workers and the public and damage neighbouring property. Work near a wall that appears unstable must stop until it has been assessed by a qualified person.

qualityStandard: The site plan records the level changes, surcharge, drainage, neighbour ground and existing walls.
Each referral trigger is recorded with the source and date of the rule checked.
The client has been told the referral in writing and no wall work has started before advice and approvals are in place.
The business's in-scope work around the wall is stated separately from the structural element.
documentationEvidence: Site plan with the level, drainage, surcharge and neighbour ground information.
Referral record with the date, the recipient, the response and the client's decision.
Approval or exemption check record, with the authority, the date checked and the source.
Photographs taken with consent, showing the existing wall and the site features.
summary: A retaining wall is a structural matter when it holds soil, carries a surcharge or affects a neighbour. Height is only one test.
Record the site features and refer the wall to an engineer or building surveyor before quoting or building.
Victoria's one-metre permit exemption and NSW's $5,000 licence threshold are confirmed for those states only.
This lesson does not grant any structural licence or approval, and the business does not design the wall.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants a wall that holds back a neighbour's ground and carries a driveway load. What is the correct decision?
options: Refer the wall to an engineer or building surveyor, because of the neighbour ground and the load, and hold the work.
Quote it as a landscape item, since the wall is under one metre and no approval is needed for a wall of that height
Build it with a standard block design from the supplier, since the design is already approved for use

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about the Victorian one-metre exemption is accurate?
options: It applies in every state and council in Australia, so no local check is needed for any wall at any site at all
It is a Victorian position from the building authority's practice note, and other states and councils are not covered here.
It means no advice is ever needed for any wall under one metre, whatever the site conditions, load or neighbour are

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a referral to an engineer include?
options: A finished structural design prepared by the crew, with the calculations and the drawings attached for the engineer
A price for building the wall, with the materials, the labour and the crew hours listed in full for the client to review today
The site description, measurements, photographs taken with consent, drainage and surcharge observations and the client's purpose.
